title: Four Foundations of Mindfulness, Part 1: Observation of Body (1)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the first section of the Sutra on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, the observation of the body, and opens with a passage from Blanche Hartman's Seeds for a Boundless Life, where she meets a riot policeman's eyes and feels a shared identity. Nomon reads the sutra's phrase "the body in the body" as an invitation to feel the body from the inside, then leads a few minutes of breathing in and out, long and short, with a wood turner at the lathe as the image. Gil Fronsdal's argument that sati is a noun closer to faith than to an activity complicates the idea of mindfulness as something a person does. Nomon closes with the cooks talking too loudly in the kitchen, which the breathing can include.

sentences.text: Good morning everybody.
Thanks for being here.

We're trying to do all the elements that we usually do in a 16-hour sesshin day in just a couple of hours, which at first seemed like it would be an easy little day, but it turns out to be sort of complicated.
Of course, we don't have to do it perfectly.
Thank goodness.
That's good.
But if you feel a little out of breath, good thing we can breathe.
Good thing.
Well, I want to continue with the topic from Wednesday evening: one of the central early Buddhist texts.
It's called the Sutra on the Four Foundations, or the Four Establishments, of Mindfulness.
Of course mindfulness is all the rage, and I'm part of the industry.
So I thought today we would continue a little more with the Sutra, but also take a step back and ask some interesting things.
What does that word even mean, mindfulness?
What are they trying to translate from Buddhist thought, and is it a good translation?
It turns out the jury's still out, and has probably always been still out, about exactly what the Buddha meant by any particular term.
The Buddha tended to use very precise language, both adapting common words of the day and creating new words.
And then later Buddhists, translating him into other languages, had to pick words and create words.
But he didn't tend to say, "I'm now going to tell you what mindfulness means.
This is what it means.
Let us practice with this."
I don't know if it was just medieval Indian discourse or what.
He didn't tell us what energy or effort or wholesomeness means.

He just used it all in context, and he would explain it in a lot of different ways, with a lot of different metaphors, and bring things up differently in different situations depending on who was listening.
And your method is figured out.
Maybe in a way that's the best teaching he could leave us: something that we're continuously having to figure out and reinvent and understand and apply.
Because it turns out, even with Buddhas appearing in the world, there's no operating manual for our life.
So if we try to treat Buddhist teachings, or anything else, as an operating manual for our life, we might be a little frustrated.
But before that, let's have a little prequel.
I've been greatly enjoying finally dipping into the book *Seeds for a Boundless Life*, the collected teachings of Blanche Hartman.
We talked quite a bit about Blanche when she passed last year, or last summer, I can't remember when.
She was one of my early teachers.
Not a very formal relationship, but I was around her a lot as a young student, and she came up here at least once to help us.
She was a very humble kind of teacher.
She never gave long, elaborate Dharma talks.
I mean, she studied and she did all the things that serious practitioners do, and she was very serious about practice.
But I remember, when I was at Tassajara Monastery in the early 90s, doing a training period there, she was the teacher.
I think she had just become one of the abbots of San Francisco Zen Center, maybe for the first time.
And it turned out that she would really have rather been working in the physical plant, fixing the plumbing and doing carpentry projects, than formal teaching, giving talks and meeting with students.
So she used to give these talks that were pretty much her saying, for half an hour, "I really don't know what I'm doing.
But I'm supposed to be on the schedule, give a talk, and have faith in the schedule, and faith in my teachers.
So I'll try to say something."
I don't really remember her saying that much, but it was inspiring nonetheless.
And then, the year I was there, there had been a long-time maintenance guy who wasn't really a formal Zen student.
He was just a very good maintenance guy, and he had been living on campus.
Tassajara is very remote.
You can't just run to the hardware store, so you have to have pretty skilled people who can figure out how to fix things.
It's off the grid: independent water system, power system, everything.
This guy, I think his name was Robert, had just left before I got there, under a cloud.
I don't know what happened, but some angry-making thing happened.
Or maybe there was a sense that they had been putting up with something that wasn't quite right for their community.
I don't know what.
Anyway, he had just left.
Then a couple of weeks into the practice period, the plumbing broke.
The plumbing for the whole place.
There was no water coming in the pipes.
I was far from a skilled plumber, or even a skilled anything.
I was a professor's son from the suburbs.
But I had spent the last couple of years in Bellingham doing odd jobs, and I was a stage technology guy in high school.
I learned a lot about carcary there.
I don't know.
Anyway, I knew bits and pieces, and it turned out, weirdly, that I was the most skilled plumber in the whole valley, in a 20-mile radius.
So I sat there working to figure this out.
It turned out they had a UV sterilizer: the water from the spring went down these long pipes and through this sort of jiggy-jaggy thing, so it would stay long enough exposed to the ultraviolet light.
And that had clogged up with sand.
It was not complicated.
It had been poorly designed, too.
Even I could tell that there was no trap, no clean-out, no way to get the sand out.
So I was taking this whole thing apart, kind of praying that I'd be able to figure out how to get it back together, or the whole community would not be able to function.
The practice period would be cancelled.
It was very high stakes.
They were very strict about the schedule, and it was a long schedule.
You got up at 3:40 or something in the morning.
Lots and lots of Zazen, not all day and all night, but lots.
So I was out there, and it felt very weird.
I worked through the work period and it was all still apart.
Then the [unclear: "hon"] starts to bring us back to the Zendo.
You've got to change and clean up, so it takes a while to get back to the Zendo.
Or the drum, I forget.
Some signal goes off.
So I'm like, oh my gosh.
Even though I'm a young pup and don't know what I'm doing, I'd better just keep working on the plumbing, even though it's time to go to the Zendo.
It just felt weird.
I was conditioned enough to know that was weird.
And so I'm working away, and who comes out to help me?
Blanche, the abbess of the whole place, in her work clothes, rolling up her sleeves, literally.
Let's do this thing.
She was quite a great person, very humble and devoted.
Anyway, I'm going to read you just one little section from her book.
She would not have had the temerity to write a book.
One of her students combed through all the recordings of all of her talks and little articles she'd written and put it together for her.
I'm sure she helped to edit it.
And that's true of a lot of Dharma books.
Anyway, somebody was asking me a little while ago what our practice says about peace.
About peacefulness.
It's certainly an interesting time in the world to ask that question.
So here's a little bit from Blanche about that.
Her editor called this the most transformative moment.
*During the Vietnam War I was a political activist.
I fought for peace.
There was some contradiction there.
There wasn't any peace in me.
I hated the people who disagreed with me.
There was a kind of war within me.
In 1968 I was just beginning to look at the way in which I was vigorously clinging to my opinions about things and denigrated others who had different opinions.
When there was a strike at San Francisco State University the police came with their masks and clubs and started poking people.
And without thinking I ducked under the hands of the people, I ducked under the held hands of people to get between the police and the students.
And I met this riot squad policeman face to face with his mask on and everything.
He was close enough to touch.
I met the policeman's eyes straight on and I had this overwhelming experience of identification, of a shared identity, of a shared experience.
This was the most transformative moment of my life.
Having this experience of shared identity with a riot squad policeman.*
*It was a real gift.
Nothing had prepared me for it.
I didn't have any conceptual basis for understanding it.
The total experience was real and incontrovertible.
I could never be the same after that moment.
My life as a political activist ended with that encounter because there was no longer anything to fight.
I couldn't fight against others anymore.
The way I described it to my friends was the police was trying to protect what he thought was good and right from the other people that he thought were trying to destroy it.
And I was doing the exact same thing.

Since I had no basis for understanding the experience of shared identity with someone whom I had considered completely other, that is a riot squad policeman, and because the experience had been so real and so powerful, I began to search for someone who could understand it.
How could a riot squad policeman and I be the same?
In my search I met Suzuki Roshi.
The way he looked at me, the first way that he looked at me, I knew that he understood.
And that's how I came, in the end, to be an ordained monastic.*
The way the rest of her life is beautiful, huh?
Of course, one of the many things I like about that story is it wasn't part of her plan, you know what I mean?
It wasn't like the next step for an activist or anything like that.
Somehow conditions were right, in her and right in the situation, and it just happened.
It just happened.
I think we have minds that are so step-wise and organized and want the next thing that's supposed to happen to happen, and why am I still feeling this way, and so on and so on.
Maybe we don't get that degree of planning and order and control.
Maybe whatever you want to call it, the universe, karma, Buddha, God, your heart, just provides the next thing when you're ready for it.
So anyway, this early sutta or sutra on mindfulness has been revered for 2,500 years, and in many ways is a root text in the 19th century vipassana revival.
The vipassana, insight movement as we know it now, is largely the result of a revival movement in Burma and Thailand in the 19th century.
So it's an important text in that movement, and also a very important text in the contemporary mindfulness movement.
One of the most successful and most well-known formats for mindfulness training, a class called mindfulness-based stress reduction, which I also teach, more or less is patterned on this ancient text.
Although the creator of it, John Kabat-Zinn, won't admit that for some reason.
I don't know why.
He claims it just came to him with flashing insight, but when you read this sutra and you think about his curriculum, it sure sounds like it lines up perfectly.
So the Buddha, at the beginning of the sutra, if you were here on Wednesday or if you remember, makes some pretty strong claims about mindfulness.
That mindfulness practice, he says, is just the most wonderful way to practice.
It helps us realize purification, overcome grief and sorrow, end pain, end anxiety.
And it really keeps us on the right path to the very end, to full awakening.
I looked up one of the Pali terms that's translated in the part about how it's the most wonderful way, and the Pali term turns out to have an element of one-directional.
You can't regress with this.
There's no going back, in a good way.
We hear "no, there's no going back," and it always seems like a bad thing.
Maybe it's a good thing.
And then he's going to explain that there are four big areas of focus for our mindfulness practice.
The way this is explained, you're mindful of something.
He says the first thing is the body.
First he gives an overall instruction which is repeated many, many times, and now he's going to give us some specifics about how to practice mindfulness of the body.
Or maybe it's better to say mindfulness in the body.
He says,
*Monks and nuns, practitioner remains established in the observation or the mindfulness of the body in the body.
The body in the body.
She should be diligent, have clear understanding, be mindful.
She should have abandoned craving and distaste.*
So let's unpack that a little bit.
And then I want to share with you what I hear from another teacher about how uncertain the exact meaning of the term mindfulness really is.
In a way that's disconcerting, but in a way it gives us a lot of freedom to practice and develop and grow.
So it's a five-part formula here, that the practitioner remains established.
When we try to establish our mindfulness of the body, we need to stay.
So it's a sustained thing.
This takes a while, right?
Years, decades, "remains established."
So there's a maintenance quality to this.
Stay, stay, stay.
At the session that I co-led in September with Jeff Kelly, he had a great little way of describing a moment in zazen.
I can't remember all the terms he used, but he said something like: first you recognize what's happening.
A twinge in the body, an angry thought, something.
You recognize something's happening.
And then you observe it, you get curious about what it is.
There's something happening, what is it?
You observe it.
And then, he said, you stay.
He described it to us like calming a dog down.
Stay, stay, stay.
So the Buddha says that here too.
Stay.
Stay in the body.
But he doesn't just say the body, he says the body in the body.
Other translations say the body in and of itself.
And this is a really central point in all of this.
Which is fun about these texts: sometimes just a little expression can be really important if you think about it.
We tend to look at everything from the outside in, right?
I'm over here looking at things, looking at my past, looking at my life.
And we do the exact same thing even with our own body.
I'm over here looking at this body.
I don't know how we do it exactly.
We conceive of ourselves as if we're in a mirror.
Like our real self is somewhere up here in the forehead, looking down.
What's going on down there?
I notice some pain.
What's with that?
I'm busy.
So this is saying: not looking at the body from the outside.
There's a way we relate to our body as if it were external to us.
And of course all these teachings are going to suggest that nothing is external to us.
Nothing whatsoever.
But most especially our own body, right?
So can we really enter into our body?
Feel our body from the inside out?
Then it says "diligent."
So stay with energy, I guess.
And all these are translations of Pali terms which we could unpack, any one of them, for many talks.
Then it says "with clear understanding."
Clear understanding.
So how can our understanding ever be totally clear, though, right?
Our understanding is always somewhat distorted by our conditioning, by our history.
So I guess we should read that as: be as clear as we can be with what's happening now.
And little by little as we practice, right, we notice more and more of the layers.
The layers of confusion and clinging and misunderstanding and perceptual mistakes.
We start to recognize that we can only really see the surface of things.
And we shouldn't assume that we know what's going on inside.
We only see the surface.
And that's true even of our own body experience.
We just see the surface.
So maybe clear understanding involves lots of curiosity, lots of humility.
And there are moments.
I think we all have moments where things do feel a little more clear, don't you think?
There's more muddled.
There's a kind of gradient of muddledness, right?
That we're always moving back and forth on.
And so, to treasure those moments of clarity.
And in the muddled moments, to recognize that's where we're at.
That our clear understanding then is: I'm really muddled and confused.
You know, life's a bear and all that.
And then he repeats "mindful" again.
So we'll get to that.
And then he makes an interesting statement, that there's this prerequisite: that we've already liberated ourselves from clinging and aversion to the world.
That's a tall order.
I think we can take that to mean really deeply, including the study of clinging and aversion.
To be able to see clinging and aversion.
To see desire.
To see distaste.
To see wanting things a different way from the way they are.
Clearly, clearly.
And that kind of teaching is easy to misunderstand, too.
Freedom or abandonment of craving and distaste doesn't mean that now we just put up with stuff.
That everything is fine the way it is.
There are certainly things that need changing.
No question, right?
And our commitment to compassion would just evaporate if we were completely passive in accepting everything.
You know, "I'm sorry you're suffering.
Bummer," right?
That's as far as we could go.
But you can accept.
You can abandon craving and distaste.
"Don't worry.
Relax.
It's no problem."
It doesn't help people, does it?
So what this means is, in each moment of experience, and remember the early Buddhists were very good at this, that was their whole project.
It was: let's simplify our lives for the rest of our lifetimes and support each other in paying attention to one moment at a time, right?
I mean, that was their plan.
And then let's see if we can analyze and understand what happens for human beings in one moment and then the next moment.
Why do we suffer?
When is there freedom and liberation?
How can we live together, right?
It wasn't a solo thing.
They lived in communities like we do.
And so this is talking about that moment-by-moment feeling and touching and knowing what's arising now.
Can I accept that what's arising now is exactly what's arising now?
And trying to resist it or grab onto it or manipulate it in that tight gut-instant way is probably not going to help me or anybody.
But then, the "but then" is important.
But then we recognize what's happening and we make a choice, right?
We make a choice.
And so the Buddha, in the Buddha's time, for instance, created little by little lots and lots of precepts, which are our topic for the afternoon.
He recognized, I mean, he could accept that the monks and nuns were human and fallible.
And he started to recognize some unwholesome patterns.
He could say, "Monks and nuns, I noticed you're doing such-and-such behavior, some of you, and it's causing such-and-such result.
So cut it out.
It's from now on a rule of training that you not do that."
And he was very sensitive to anything that would create disharmony or trouble within the monastic community and within the lay community around them.
For instance, when they went on their daily begging rounds, he noticed that some monks were only going to the rich households.
And there are a couple of possible motivations for that.
One is actually quite generous.
If you think of this at first, the generous motivation would be to give those who have the most means more opportunity to practice generosity.
It's very generous.
Of course, the other one we think of right away, because we have minds that are pretty much revolved around getting stuff, right.
That's why we think of that so quickly.
Oh, the greedy monks.
They knew they'd get better food.
Then he also noticed, and realized that's no good, some monks and nuns going only to the poor houses for the same reasons in reverse.
He realized that's no good either.
So he made a rule of training: don't choose.
Just go.
I don't know which neighborhood to go to, but just walk.
Let go of all that.
Just walk.
See where you end up.
And so now he's going to give us a few suggestions about how to actually do this in regard to the body.
What the teacher, whom I want to quote in a few moments, says is that he doesn't exactly say how to do mindfulness.
This entire sutra, the most important sutra on mindfulness, never says, here's how to do mindfulness.

But he offers some practices in each of these four big categories, the first being the body, that we can only assume are designed for mindfulness: to increase the possibility of mindfulness being here, to facilitate mindfulness, to create good conditions for mindfulness.
So here's what he says about the body.
*How, amongst the nuns, does a practitioner remain established in mindfulness of the body in the body?
She goes to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty room, sits down cross-legged in the lotus position, holding his body straight, and establishes mindfulness in front of him.*
Interesting image.
Establishes mindfulness in front of him.
*She then breathes in.* Okay, next thing you do, breathe in.
Okay, good, breathe in.
*She then breathes in, aware that she is breathing in.
She breathes out, aware that she is breathing out.*
That's the first instruction.
Should we try it for a minute?
Let's practice.
This is so simple, right?
Our minds are so complicated, we're like, well, wait a minute, where's the advanced?
There's no advanced.
Let's settle ourselves for a minute.
We're just doing this in zazen, more or less, I'm sure.
The funny thing about a room full of people doing zazen is that one has no idea what's going on, really.
But let's establish mindfulness in front of us.
Different commentators argue forever about what that means, mindfulness in front of us, but maybe it's a feeling that we're setting a sort of reminder sign right in front of us.
Like we're looking at an internal reminder that we place there: remember to be mindful, because the root of mindfulness actually is remembering.
So we're setting our intention in front of us, and we're in relationship to that intention, which we imagine to be right in front of us in space.
So, breathing in, knowing: what does it actually feel like to breathe in?
Breathing out, can we know, through the whole breath cycle, the feeling in the body of breathing out?
What a continuous opportunity for mindfulness practice that is.
We're always either breathing in, or breathing out, or for a moment, a moment of pause as it turns around, which has always been my favorite place to practice, actually.
So let's try for a few minutes just awareness of breathing.
And awareness of breathing need not be tight awareness.
It should be stable, but it can be broad.
Able to feel the breathing while hearing the rain and my words, while feeling the body, while aware of the space around us.
And that stable attention is also able to notice when the focus skitters away, a thought, something, and coming back.
This broad stable awareness can actually include the mind wandering.
The mind wandering is not a distraction, but just part of this big experience of being a person breathing, being a body in the body breathing.
Including even the so-called distraction of the mind.
Breathing with that too.
Okay, great.
Feel free to adjust the body a little bit.
Shrug your shoulders, or whatever you like.
I remember when Norman Fischer first came here, in the early 90s, when meditation was not so much the rage.
Nobody had heard of mindfulness, really.
The Dalai Lama was not yet a rock star.
It's hard to think how that's all changed.
We would usually try to set him up to give a public talk, because nobody knew about this little thing we were doing in this little rented room somewhere.
And nobody really much knew who Norman Fischer was either.
But we would rent a library room or something and have him give a talk.
He would almost always begin the talk with a few minutes of just breathing, which now seems like a totally normal thing to me.
But at the time it seemed like, are you sure?
You want to do that?
That's kind of weird.
These people didn't sign up for a meditation thing.
They just want to hear a talk.
I'm sure I'm saying, well, what's cool about it is something always happens.
Something always happens for every person in that room, if you just stop and breathe for a minute.
We don't need to make a big deal about it, but we can draw their attention to that fact and see if they find that interesting.
That's true, don't you think?
Here we are in the middle of a Zen center, in the middle of a Zen retreat, and I bet you something just happened.
We're not really doing anything.
Just breathing.
There's another recent book, and this is a book day, which is part of how I'm getting out of not really preparing very much.
So this was Blanche Hartman's book, because I was a little busy preparing for the ceremony.
There's another interesting new book called *What's Wrong with Mindfulness?
And What Isn't?* Although the "What's Wrong with Mindfulness" is in great, big, bright type, and "What Isn't" is in small, low-contrast type.
So the biases of the authors are pretty clear.
Although, actually, the authors don't get to design the covers, so it might not be their choice.
So here's a little bit from a wonderful teacher named Gil Fronsdal.
Gil is an interesting teacher in California, because he both did extensive Soto Zen training in our lineage, and then he went on to become a Vipassana teacher.
So he's got real deep roots in the two main, well, I don't know what the Tibetans are left out, but two of the major strains of American Buddhism.
He's going to talk a little bit about the term that's being translated as mindfulness.
And it's interesting how he says, well, we don't really know.
He'll say it better than me, though.
Gil wrote:

*In the early Pali discourses, the concept of Sati,* so Sati is the word in Pali, being translated as mindfulness, *the concept of Sati is used in two broad, overlapping ways, the mental faculty of Sati and the practice of Sati.
The distinct role in the course of meditation of these two aspects of Sati is often obscured because it's easy to conflate them,* to mix them together.

*As a mental facility, Sati is one of the five mental faculties, or Indrayas, that is faith, energy, Sati, concentration, and wisdom.* So one of the famous core lists, if you remember way back, we studied a list of 37 called the Bodhicitta, Bodhipakashika, now I forget the term, but there's a core list of 37, and this is part of that list, five mental faculties.
Then he goes on:
*It is true, as is true with many terms, the Buddhist discourses do not provide a detailed definition or explanation of the faculty of Sati.
However, to understand what this faculty is, we have to rely on how the word is used in the ancient texts.
One way of understanding what Sati might be is through the relationship one can have with it.
How do you relate to this faculty?
In the Buddhist teaching, this is described as followed,* and he lists five things.

*One possesses Sati,* possesses mindfulness, *one is endowed with Sati,* endowed with mindfulness, *one has purity of Sati,* so has a pure mindfulness, *one is established in Sati,* so established in, rooted in mindfulness, *and one abides in Sati,* one abides in mindfulness, like lives in mindfulness.
*In the first three of these statements,* possesses, endowed, has purity, the first three statements, *Sati appears to be something one has, and the last two is a state within which one is.
Nowhere does the Buddha specifically instruct others to actively apply or do Sati.
Sati, in this case, is a noun and not a verb.

There's one passage where the Buddha says he arouses Sati in his monastic disciples, but while this may mean he instructs them to do Sati, it would also mean that he himself evokes the state of Sati in them.*
It was very moving to be with the Buddha.
*Overall, the discourses give the impression that Sati is an important factor that a person possesses, but is not a mental activity a person intentionally engages in.
In this sense, the faculty of Sati may be similar to the faculty of faith.* All the Zen students are like, oh no, faith!
Which is a core Buddhist idea, actually.
Faith, or maybe trust, is easier to map it to trust.
*While one can have faith and one can develop faith, faith is not something one does.* How do you do faith?
How do you do trust?
You can do things that encourage it, that support it, but you can't make it happen.
*So Sati may be like faith,* like trust.
*The words Sati and Sadha, the word for faith, are nouns, referring to faculties one possesses or can be established in, not something that is actively practiced.

So, when the Buddha instructs monastics to make an effort to develop Sati, or to evaluate whether it has [unclear: "developed a noun"], he's not telling them to engage in a particular activity called mindfulness, rather he's telling them to engage in activities that strengthen the faculty of Sati.
This is why the Buddha explains the development of Sati through activities other than Sati.* In other words, the Sati is a result of other practices.
So that's interesting.
Of course, it's a little problematic for me because I go all around the place telling people that mindfulness is a verb, and he says here Sati is a noun, that mindfulness is a process.
It helps us to engage in life as a process, and I think this is really true.
But maybe my predecessors in the mindfulness movement, chiefly John Kabat-Zinn, sort of distorted the original meaning a little bit.
But you know what?
That's what we do.
The trick is: can we do it for the good, right?
And know that we're doing it.
So let's go on a little longer with the text, and my intention is to continue with this text for the rest of the month, in November.
And maybe you won't be able to get me to stop talking about it in Rohatsu 2, I don't know.
But regardless of whether we know what mindfulness is, it doesn't matter.
That's the other problem for us.
We really, really, really, really, really, really want to know what does that mean?
I'm not going to do that.
I don't know what it means.
Which is a little flummoxing for some people at first with our whole Zen rigmarole, right?
What's all that mean?
Somebody told me the other day that he thought that the very structure of a silent retreat was an archaic form that should be abandoned.
Well, he was a very smart, well-reasoned guy, and he'd been thinking about this for some days of silence.
And I was a little taken aback, and I thanked him for his feedback.
And I meant it.
I really want to think about that.
Like, archaic, huh?
It's like, yeah, we modern people, we learn by dialogue and inquiry and engagement with each other.
Community.
I tried to say, well, it seems like there is all that without talking all the time.
I have to admit I got a little bit defensive, but I did manage to ask him, a perfectly nice person: what are you noticing in this silent retreat that you signed up for, came to?
What are you noticing that feels good, that's beneficial?
And all the things that he told me, I can't un-imagine happening without silence.

Like he said, well, I was walking, doing walking meditation on the lawn, and I suddenly noticed that there's a thin layer of spider webs just running across the top of the leaf blades, and then the light was just such that it was all lit up like jewels.
Gosh, it's the most beautiful thing I ever saw.
So anyway, we shouldn't have too much fun at his expense, but we want to know why, right?
We want to have a good reason, and if we have a good reason why it's not okay, then we're pretty convinced of our reasons, right?
It could be archaic.
